chapter.name: Quadratic Equations
chapter.blurb: Defining a quadratic equation in standard form, representing real-life situations as one, solving by factorisation and by the quadratic formula, and using the discriminant to decide the nature of the roots and to solve applied problems.

scope_in.item: Definition of a quadratic equation and its standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a not equal to 0); checking whether a given equation, after simplification, is quadratic
Representing real-life situations (areas, ages, products of numbers, speed-distance-time, cost of production) as a quadratic equation in standard form
Meaning of a root/solution of a quadratic equation (a(alpha)^2 + b(alpha) + c = 0) and verifying a given value by substitution; a quadratic equation has at most two roots
Solving a quadratic equation by factorisation: splitting the middle term and equating each linear factor to zero, including equations with surd coefficients and repeated (equal) roots
The quadratic formula x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a and using it to find real roots

The discriminant b^2 - 4ac and the three-way classification of the nature of roots (two distinct real roots, two equal real roots, no real roots), including finding an unknown coefficient for equal roots
Forming a quadratic equation from a word problem, solving it by factorisation or the formula, and accepting or rejecting each root against the real-world conditions of the problem

scope_out.item: Solving a quadratic equation by completing the square as a general, named method
scope_out.reason: This rationalised edition removed the separate completing-the-square section; only factorisation and the ready-made quadratic formula are taught as solution methods, and the formula's own derivation is not walked through for students to repeat

scope_out.item: Sum and product of the roots (alpha + beta = -b/a, alpha * beta = c/a) as named results
scope_out.reason: Not stated or used anywhere in this chapter

scope_out.item: Complex or imaginary roots when the discriminant is negative
scope_out.reason: The book states only 'no real roots' in this case and never introduces a number system beyond the reals here

scope_out.item: Graphical method: sketching y = ax^2 + bx + c and reading the roots off as x-intercepts
scope_out.reason: Not part of this chapter; there is no graph or coordinate-plane treatment of quadratic equations here. Confirmed by rendering the one page with no text layer (printed p.48): it is a blank 'NOTE' page ruled for the student's own notes, not a graph or diagram

scope_out.item: Forming a quadratic equation when only its roots are given (the reverse construction x^2 - (sum)x + (product) = 0)
Equations of degree higher than 2 reduced to quadratic form by substitution (e.g. biquadratic equations)
scope_out.reason: Outside this chapter; every equation here is quadratic after at most one simplification pass

scope_out.item: The historical figures named in the introduction (Babylonians, Euclid, Brahmagupta, Sridharacharya, Al-Khwarizmi, Abraham bar Hiyya Ha-Nasi)
scope_out.reason: Mentioned only as scene-setting narrative on pages 38-39; not developed into a testable point, so kept out of the question grid rather than tested as trivia

concepts.name: Quadratic Equations: Definition and Standard Form
concepts.description: The general standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 of a quadratic equation in one variable, and how to tell whether a given equation is quadratic after simplifying it.
concepts.idea: An equation is quadratic when, after simplifying both sides fully, the variable's highest power is exactly 2.
concepts.rule: ax^2 + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a is not equal to 0, is the standard form of a quadratic equation in x. Any equation p(x) = 0, where p(x) is a polynomial of degree 2, is a quadratic equation.
concepts.example: (x - 2)^2 + 1 = 2x - 3 simplifies to x^2 - 6x + 8 = 0, which is quadratic. But x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x - 2) simplifies to x + 12 = 0, degree 1, so it is not quadratic.

concepts.name: Roots of a Quadratic Equation: Meaning and Verification
concepts.description: What it means for a number to be a root of a quadratic equation, and verifying a given value by substitution.
concepts.idea: A root is a value of the variable that makes the equation true; substitute it back in to check.
concepts.rule: A real number alpha is a root of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a not equal to 0) if a(alpha)^2 + b(alpha) + c = 0. The roots of the equation are the same as the zeroes of the polynomial ax^2 + bx + c. A quadratic equation has at most two roots.
concepts.example: For 2x^2 - 3x + 1 = 0, putting x = 1 gives 2(1)^2 - 3(1) + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0, so x = 1 is a root.

concepts.name: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorisation
concepts.description: Finding the roots of a quadratic equation by splitting the middle term and factorising into two linear factors.
concepts.idea: Split the middle term into two terms whose product equals a*c (the product of the outer coefficients) and whose sum equals b, then group in pairs to pull out a common factor twice.
concepts.rule: If ax^2 + bx + c can be written as a product of two linear factors, the roots are found by setting each factor equal to 0. A repeated linear factor gives one root counted twice (equal roots).

concepts.name: The Quadratic Formula

concepts.idea: Completing the square on the general equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 once and for all gives a ready-made formula for the roots of any quadratic equation.
concepts.rule: The roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a not equal to 0) are given by x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a), provided b^2 - 4ac is greater than or equal to 0.

concepts.name: The Discriminant and Nature of Roots
concepts.description: The discriminant b^2 - 4ac of a quadratic equation and what its sign tells us about the number and type of real roots.
concepts.idea: The sign of b^2 - 4ac under the square root decides, without fully solving, whether the equation has two different real roots, two equal real roots, or none.
concepts.rule: For ax^2 + bx + c = 0, the discriminant is D = b^2 - 4ac. Two distinct real roots if D > 0; two equal real roots if D = 0; no real roots if D < 0.

concepts.name: Applications: Forming and Solving Quadratic Equations
concepts.description: Using a quadratic equation end to end on a word problem: form it, solve it, and accept or reject each root using the problem's own conditions.
concepts.idea: Model the situation as a quadratic equation, solve it by factorisation or the formula, then check both roots against the real-world conditions and reject any that do not make sense.
concepts.rule: After solving, discard roots that give a negative length, age, speed, or count, or any value the situation rules out; keep only the admissible root(s).
concepts.example: A pole on a circular park of diameter 13 m has distances differing by 7 m from two diametrically opposite gates; this gives x^2 + 7x - 60 = 0 with roots x = 5 and x = -12, and x = -12 is rejected since a distance cannot be negative, so the pole is 5 m from one gate and 12 m from the other.
